This city in central Bolivia lies in a valley of the same name in the Andes. It is the capital of the Cochabamba department and Bolivia's third-largest city. Cochabamba is known as the "City of Eternal Spring" because of its springlike temperatures throughout the year.

The city is home to La Cancha, described as the largest open-air market in South America, which operates seven days a week. You can find almost anything here, from magical talismans and love charms to LCD televisions and music players.

The city's main attraction is the Cristo de la Concordia statue on top of San Pedro Hill, standing 33 meters tall. Visitors can climb inside it and enjoy panoramic views over Cochabamba. Several colonial-era buildings have survived around Plaza 14 de Septiembre.

## Colón: Panama's Colonial Charm!

One of the country's best-known cities, Colón prospered during the colonial era and retains some of its charm today, despite signs of neglect.

## Colón: A City of Beautiful Beaches!

Located on the ocean, with beautiful beaches and a well-developed tourism infrastructure, Colón attracts visitors looking for a leisurely holiday. Those who enjoy nightlife will also find numerous bars and discos. Several colonial-era churches remain in the city. The surrounding tropical forests fill the air with distinctive scents and make staying here especially pleasant.

### Colonia del Sacramento: The Romance of Uruguay!

Once a port used by smugglers, the city still evokes the romance of that bygone era.

## Holidays in Colonia del Sacramento

### Colonia del Sacramento: A Welcoming City for Travelers!

Narrow cobbled streets wind between small houses, each with stories to tell from the town's past. From the top of a small hill, you can enjoy wonderful views of the Río de la Plata. The town has several relatively old churches. Numerous bars and restaurants, small cozy cafés and nightclubs offer plenty of opportunities to enjoy the nightlife.

### Copán: One of the Most Beautiful Maya Cities!

Copán was once one of the most beautiful and important cities of the Maya, one of the great ancient cultures of the Americas. Over 400 years, the Maya people of Copán transformed a small valley in western Honduras into a great city, building pyramids, temples and plazas, carving intricate statues of kings, gods and animals, and decorating the structures with beautiful colored stucco. The ceremonial center at the heart of the city contained some of the finest examples of Maya architecture and art, examples of which could also be found throughout the city.

Each city of the Maya world is known for a particular specialty. Tikal in Guatemala, for example, is famous for the extraordinary height of its pyramids. Copán is celebrated for both the number and the quality of carved stone sculptures that adorned the plazas and temples of its ceremonial center. Archaeologists have described it as the most "artistic" of all Maya cities.

## A Journey into the Maya Past

### What to See in Copán

Today this is a charming place among vivid green mountains, with small streets, welcoming cafés and bars, vine-covered houses, friendly people and fresh mountain air. The ruins were discovered in 1570. Several tourist attractions can be visited in the surrounding area, including the Archaeological Park, the ruins of Quiriguá, Santa Ana and Lake Izabal.

Córdoba is Argentina's second-largest city. Its colonial architectural monuments are better preserved than almost anywhere else in Argentina, lending the city its old-world charm. Founded in the 16th century, it soon became a "colonial capital." Its location in the heart of Argentina makes Córdoba a convenient starting point for travel to other cities and across the country. The University of San Carlos was founded here and is described as the first university in Argentina and the second in South America. The city's cathedrals and churches are among its most interesting sights, while the Provincial History Museum is considered Argentina's leading historical museum. With seven universities today, Córdoba is an educational center of the country, a role reflected in its cultural life. In 2006, it was named the cultural capital of South America. Córdoba conveys a sense of history and a distinctive identity. From the ensemble of seventeenth-century Jesuit buildings known as Manzana Jesuítica and the underground Jesuit crypts to Argentina's oldest university, the Cabildo (town hall) on Plaza San Martín, and numerous historic churches, its landmarks bear witness to a long history.

Today Córdoba also has modern buildings, shopping centers, new residential neighborhoods, entertainment venues and a lively nightlife. The climate is temperate, with plenty of sunshine. The surrounding area is rich in historical landmarks, including the Church of the Compañía de Jesús, the colonial Jesuit estates of Jesús María, Santa Catalina, La Candelaria and Alta Gracia. These form part of UNESCO World Heritage sites. In the northern part of the province is the natural and archaeological area of Cerro Colorado, once a center of the Comechingones Indigenous people. Caves decorated with ancient paintings preserve traces of their culture. The Punilla Valley, with its mountainous and hilly terrain, rivers and beautiful scenery, is a destination for outdoor recreation, with numerous routes for excursions.
